titol: Why can a trillion-dollar company wobble because of its boss?
explicacio: Some companies depend so heavily on one person, often the founder, that their future is tied to that person's. This is called key-person risk. If that person leaves, falls ill or is caught up in a scandal, investors start asking who will make the decisions and whether the strategy will survive, and the share price suffers. That's why large companies have a board of directors that oversees management and should have a successor lined up.
exemple: Nvidia fell 8% after hours on Wednesday, to about $160. Someone holding 50 shares, previously worth about $174 each ($8,700 in total), saw them drop to about $8,000 within hours: roughly $700 less, without the company selling a single chip fewer.
economia: When a big company wobbles over a leadership problem, investment decisions, hiring and supplier deals can stall. That's why investors value good corporate governance: clear rules, independent directors and a succession plan.
en_una_frase: The more a company depends on a single person, the riskier it is for those who have put their money into it.
termes: Key-person risk; Board of directors; Corporate governance; Market capitalisation; Share
noticia: Nvidia plunges after hours as board reportedly prepares to oust Jensen Huang

titol: Why can a single tenth of a point of inflation knock the stock market?
explicacio: Markets don't react to data, but to the gap between the data and what was expected. Before each release, analysts make a forecast, and share and bond prices already reflect it. If the figure matches, almost nothing happens; if it surprises, investors have to redo their sums all at once. On Tuesday, US prices were expected to rise 0.3% in a month and they rose 0.4%: it looked small, but it made markets treat a Fed rate hike as a certainty.
exemple: A tenth of a point a month is not small: if prices rise 0.3% every month, they rise 3.7% in a year; at 0.4% a month, 4.9%. That's the difference between uncomfortable inflation and worrying inflation.
economia: Expectations set the price of money before central banks act: if markets think rates will rise, bond yields and loan rates rise in advance. For businesses, that means financing a factory or a new hire gets more expensive from day one, not when the official decision arrives.
en_una_frase: In markets, what counts is not whether data are good or bad, but whether they are better or worse than expected.
termes: Market expectations; Inflation; Fed; Bond yield; Basis point
noticia: US inflation surprises on the upside again in October

concepte: The price of a stock market listing
titol: Why has Anthropic had to redo its numbers before going public?
explicacio: When a company goes public, it sells shares to outside investors for the first time. Beforehand, a group of banks asks big investors how much they would be willing to pay and proposes a price range, for example between $70 and $80 a share. If demand is strong, the final price ends up at the top of the range or even above it; if investors are hesitant, the company has to lower the price or wait. The price per share, multiplied by all the company's shares, gives its valuation: what the market thinks it is worth.
exemple: If Anthropic sells 867 million shares at $80, it raises about $69.3 billion. If it has to sell them at $70, it raises about $60.7 billion: a difference of just $10 a share means about $8.7 billion less.
economia: Going public is one of the ways companies find money to grow: building factories or data centres and hiring people. When the market is nervous and prices fall, companies raise less or postpone their plans, and that can slow investment across entire sectors.
en_una_frase: On the stock market, a company isn't worth what it says it is, but what investors are willing to pay for its shares.
termes: Stock market listing; Price range; Valuation; Share; Market capitalisation
noticia: Anthropic withdraws the price of its stock market listing, which aimed to raise up to $69.3bn

titol: Why can your mortgage go up if the ECB hasn't raised rates?
explicacio: The Euribor is the interest rate at which Europe's big banks lend each other money for one year, and most variable-rate mortgages in Spain are linked to it: you pay the Euribor plus a fixed spread agreed with your bank. The Euribor doesn't wait for the ECB: it moves with what markets think the ECB will do. This week the ECB kept its rate at 2.50%, but because investors expect a hike in December, the Euribor is already at 3.29%, more than a point higher than a year ago.
exemple: On a €167,000 mortgage over 25 years at Euribor + 0.75%, this November's annual review would take the monthly payment from about €786 to about €880.
en_una_frase: The Euribor gets ahead of the ECB: if the market expects rate hikes, mortgages get more expensive before they happen.
termes: Euribor; Spread; Interest rate; ECB; Variable-rate mortgage
noticia: The ECB holds the deposit rate at 2.50% and the Euribor rises again
economia: For the economy, a higher Euribor means more expensive credit for everyone: families buy fewer homes and businesses think twice before borrowing to invest or hire. That's exactly what the ECB wants when it's trying to curb inflation, but if it brakes too hard, the economy can slow down more than it should.
